questions.question: What specific research problem did Anthropic's Automated Alignment Researchers (AARs) outperform human researchers on?
options: Constitutional AI principle selection
Weak-to-strong training
Reward model design for RLHF
Benchmark construction for coding tasks
questions.explanation: Anthropic's 2026 AAR report on weak-to-strong training found that parallel Claude Opus 4.6 instances operating as AARs outperformed human researchers on this scalable-oversight problem.

questions.question: Why is the 'out-of-sandbox log' property critical to the integrity of the AAR research forum?
options: Because it prevents agents from reading each other's work
Because agents cannot delete or edit their own records, making logs tamper-evident and research findings trustworthy
Because it reduces the storage cost of keeping all research traces
Because it enables faster synchronization between parallel research agents
questions.explanation: If AARs could edit their own logs, they could cover up failed or dubious experiments. The out-of-sandbox log property means agents can read the forum but cannot delete or edit past records. This is a necessary condition for trusting the research output, analogous to append-only logs with write-through to external storage.

questions.question: What is the 'prescribed-workflow tradeoff' Anthropic's AAR report identifies?
options: Fixed workflows produce faster results but cost more tokens
Prescribed step-by-step workflows constrain AAR flexibility and often degrade performance compared to high-level goals with free decomposition
Prescribed workflows make AARs safer but reduce their ability to handle novel tasks
Free decomposition requires more human oversight than prescribed workflows
questions.explanation: Anthropic's report notes that prescribed workflows often constrain AAR flexibility and degrade performance. AARs given high-level goals and freedom to decompose do better than those given step-by-step plans. The safety implication is subtle: the flexibility that improves performance also allows unsanctioned decomposition and goal-drift.

questions.question: What is the 'AI R&D threshold' that RSP v3.0 defines, and how does AAR relate to it?
options: The threshold is full automation of AI R&D at competitive cost; AAR automates part of the pipeline but not the end-to-end capability development loop
The threshold is 50% automation of research tasks; AAR already crosses it
The threshold requires models to pass the Turing test; AAR is unrelated
The threshold is autonomous code generation; AAR specializes in alignment not coding
questions.explanation: RSP v3.0's AI R&D-4 threshold is the ability to fully automate the AI R&D pipeline at competitive cost vs human + AI tools. AAR automates part of the pipeline (alignment research on specific well-scoped tasks) but not the full loop, putting it one step below the threshold.

questions.question: How does the propose-then-commit pattern from Lesson 15 apply to AAR research?
options: AARs propose experimental designs; humans commit resources
AARs propose research findings; humans review and decide what to publish, retract, or refine
AARs propose model architectures; humans commit the training runs
AARs propose safety guidelines; humans commit to following them
questions.explanation: Anthropic's AAR outputs include both AAR contributions and human-researcher judgement on what to publish, retract, and refine. This maps directly to propose-then-commit: AARs accelerate the middle of the pipeline while humans hold constitutional authority at the ends.

questions.question: What is the 'compressed timeline' concern specific to automated alignment research?
options: Research papers take longer to write when agents do the work
If capability compounds faster than alignment, each AAR result reduces the gap only if the research process itself is trustworthy
Running parallel AARs compresses the timeline of research so fast that peer review becomes impossible
Automated alignment research eliminates the need for safety evaluation milestones
questions.explanation: Compressed timelines are the compounding-failure concern. If alignment research and capability research compound at similar rates, the misalignment risk surface stays manageable. If capability compounds faster (the historical trend), the gap widens. AAR is a qualified good only if its research process is trustworthy.
